gdp.title: Has Fiscal Policy Adjusted To A World Of Higher Interest Rates?
gdp.quote: The benign reading of higher real rates is that they reflect stronger expected growth, in which case r minus g might not have moved much. There’s some support for this in the UK. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in the three months to August, the eighth consecutive three-month rise, and was 1.8 per cent higher than a year earlier, comfortably above most estimates of trend growth. Last month, the ONS also revised up post-crisis productivity growth from 0.7 to 1.3 per cent a year. But that revision came from lower estimates of hours worked rather than higher output, so GDP is unchanged and the implications for future growth are unclear. GDP growth so far this year is running close to our pre-war NIESR February forecast of 1.4 per cent, significantly stronger than the forecast we made once the war had begun. Is that telling us that the underlying growth capacity is stronger than we thought, perhaps because the AI capex boom is lifting growth everywhere? Or that the effects of the war have been smaller than feared, or have yet to be felt in full (inflation in the UK won’t peak until the new year).

unemp.title: The Budget should not price young people out of work
unemp.quote: If you raise the price of a worker whose tasks a machine can do, some of that work can move to the machine. In 2017 it was older factory workers. In 2026 it is younger professional workers, and also possibly school leavers on tills and counters that self-service machines can replace. In fact, the Bank of England’s agents report warehouse operators looking to automate after recent labour cost inflation, and retail and hospitality have shed 117,000 employees in a year, more than all other industries combined. Out-of-work benefit claims have risen most among 18 to 20-year-olds, from 7.2 to 9.4 per cent between 2022 and 2025. Meanwhile the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate. A price rise of that size, for workers who have just become substitutable, lies outside anything in the Commission’s known evidence base.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: Our data and knowledge is simply not good enough to be very confident about the fiscal consequences of the recent reductions in net migration. The £7bn cost is almost certainly a large over-estimate and it is conceivable there is actually a benefit. Even if the reductions in net migration have a small fiscal cost over the forecast horizon they are of migrants who, on average, are likely to be fiscally negative over their lifetime. Immigration of this type is akin to borrowing – it gives you more resources today at the expense of less in the future. Where fiscal rules constrain literal borrowing this migration as disguised borrowing has been an attractive policy for successive governments. But this would not be the first government if it succumbed to the temptations of short-termism.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: The March 2024 OBR estimates also do not take into account who the migrants are, how much they work and how much they earn. They assume migrants are the same as the average Brit of the same age and sex (broadly consistent with the data we have). But migrants vary a lot in their employment and earnings, so it’s important to think about the types of migrants that make up the reduction in net migration. The big reductions in migration have come from falls in care workers and their dependents, the dependents of Masters’ students, some family, nurses, and some other work migrants (mostly the lower-paid). Since the 2024 OBR report we know the first three groups have low levels of earnings, in some cases not much above minimum wage and that lower-paid migrants are more likely to stay. Taking account of this would again reduce the cost of the reduction in migration, though how much is uncertain, given the data. What’s more, nurses’ salaries are paid by the Government, so there is an extra expenditure associated with them.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: First, the OBR itself came to recognise that migration required more public expenditure that its March 2024 estimates implied if it was not to have some implicit austerity. In their September 2024 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, the OBR argued that extra public investment of £20k per person would be needed to maintain the public sector capital stock (the hospitals, schools roads etc) in per capita terms (though they also gave some reasons why this might be too high). earn.title: My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth?
earn.quote: It wouldn’t be a Mike TOTC without some mention of inequality, and yesterday’s ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings data dump gave us the definitive take on earnings inequality, with data now up to 2026. The headline was that the share of workers in low pay failed to fall for the first time in 15 years, but Chart of the Week takes a closer look at overall pay inequality, measured by the 90:10 ratio (where higher numbers mean more unequal pay) for hourly pay and weekly earnings. Women’s weekly earnings have long been less equal than men’s – due to their higher share of part-time workers – but the genders have been slowly converging since this series began in 2002. More recently, overall earnings inequality has ticked up across the board, after a decade of decline. This is partly because the National Living Wage, which used to outpace median pay, is now only keeping pace with it, but is also because high earners are pulling away: weekly pay for the 90th percentile grew by 7.3 per cent in nominal terms this year (to reach £1,433 a week), against just 1.1 per cent at the 10th percentile. Among men, earnings inequality is now at its joint highest on record (alongside 2014), thanks to increasing numbers with a low weekly paycheck (the 10th percentile fell in cash terms from £309 in 2025 to £301 in 2026).

ecb.quote: Of all the sovereigns facing rising rates, France may face the biggest challenge. Today’s bond market is exposing a French economic problem that has been building for years. France must grapple with structurally higher long-term interest rates in the context of a very weak fiscal starting point and a longstanding growth problem. Until now, French government bonds have enjoyed something close to a mini-exorbitant privilege, with yields just a little higher than Germany and in any case too big to fail. Public debt climbed from around the Maastricht-compatible 60 percent of GDP at the birth of the euro to 120 percent today, without governments being forced to confront the sustainability of public debt and the French social model.

fiscal.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
fiscal.quote: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged. […] Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

fiscal.title: John Healey’s underwhelming budget punts big decisions into 2027
fiscal.quote: Many small changes could have cumulated to a big overall change in fiscal stance. But they mostly cancelled out. On the forecast, the cost to the exchequer from slightly lower real growth is offset by higher tax receipts, helped in large part by tax thresholds remaining frozen. Higher interest rates means forecast borrowing increased, and Healey allowed the bigger fiscal buffer Reeves had built up to fall to absorb that shock. That leaves him only a 56% chance, based on past forecast errors, of meeting his main fiscal rule of a current budget surplus in 2029/30, down from 59% at the last budget.

fiscal.title: The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth
fiscal.quote: The Chancellor’s first Budget had to do three things at once in a challenging and uncertain context: maintain a credible fiscal buffer against future shocks, support households struggling with a prolonged cost of living crisis, and nurture the green shoots of growth that have emerged despite global headwinds (or, more like storms – as the Chancellor put it). […] On the first two, the OBR confirmed that the Chancellor is forecast to meet the fiscal rules by 2029-30 with headroom of £15bn against the stability rule (rising to £22bn in 2030-31) which seems reasonable given the context and market expectations; and a package of household support has been set out to provide “breathing space” (though this could have been better targeted). The harder test is the third. Increasing the quantity and quality of public investment, measures to boost business investment, and a successful programme of devolution will be crucial for shaping prosperity.

tariff.title: Trump Tariffs: Tracking the Economic Impact of the Trump Trade War
tariff.quote: In calendar year 2024, the US federal government collected $79 billion in customs duties. Collections rose to $264 billion in calendar year 2025 after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of new tariffs. In February 2026, however, the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, and the illegally collected revenues (plus interest) were required to be returned to importers. Refunds of the illegally collected duties accelerated in May 2026, offsetting customs duties revenue collections such that the government refunded more than it brought in.

tariff.title: Trump Tariffs: Tracking the Economic Impact of the Trump Trade War
tariff.quote: According to the World Bank, the US’s weighted average applied tariff was 1.5 percent in 2022. We estimate that under the new US tariffs imposed and scheduled to take effect in 2026, the applied rate rises to 11.8 percent. In the days prior to the Supreme Court’s Learning Resources decision, we estimate the applied tariff rate was 14.8 percent, and that it fell to 10.8 percent under the temporary Section 122 replacement tariffs. The applied tariff rate under the current tariffs is below its peak reached prior to the Court decision.
